name: Broken Here
author: brokenhere

sections.description:
Somebody finds something broken on your site: a client, a colleague, a customer. They press Report issue, write one sentence and send it.

Your team gets a report with everything they never typed:

  • a screenshot of the page, with password fields blurred before it is taken
  • the page’s address, the browser, the operating system and the screen size
  • the element on the page, if they pointed at one
  • the JavaScript errors and console warnings from your site’s own code
  • the requests that failed around the moment they reported

Nobody has to explain what they were doing, and nobody has to ask them what browser they use.

Nobody needs an account to report

The people reporting write a sentence and press Send. No sign-up, no email address required, nothing to install. That is the point: the person who finds the bug is rarely the person who can fix it.

Made for sites you build for someone else

Send your client the site, and their “the form doesn’t work” arrives with the error that stopped it. Before launch, show the button only to people logged in to the site, so your client can report and visitors see nothing. After launch, turn it on for everyone.

Where the reports go

To your inbox on brokenhere.com, as an email to your team if they want one, and into the tracker your team already uses once you connect it. A developer can hand a report to a coding agent, which opens a fix for your team to review.

Light on your pages

The button loads after your page and never delays it. The screenshot tool is only downloaded when somebody starts a report.

Getting started

  1. Install and activate the plugin.
  2. Create a free account on brokenhere.com and add your site.
  3. Paste your project key under Settings › Broken Here.

Broken Here is free for one site. Plans for more sites are on brokenhere.com/pricing.

External services

This plugin connects your site to Broken Here (https://brokenhere.com), a bug-reporting service. Nothing is loaded from it until you save a project key.

With a key saved, the pages of your site (every page, or only pages seen by people logged in to WordPress, as you choose) load the Broken Here widget, https://brokenhere.com/w.js, in the visitor’s browser. When it loads, the widget asks brokenhere.com for your project’s settings; that request says which site it came from, which is how your project’s Setup shows that the button is live.

When somebody sends a report, the widget sends Broken Here:

  • what they wrote, and their name and email only if they give them;
  • the page’s address, with the value of any parameter named like a secret (a token, a password, a session) replaced in the browser;
  • the browser, operating system, window size and language;
  • a screenshot of the page, with password fields and any area you choose blurred in the browser first, and any images they attach;
  • the element they pointed at, if they did;
  • recent JavaScript errors and console warnings and errors from your site’s own code;
  • recent and failed network requests: the address without its query string, the method, the status and how long it took.

Request bodies are sent only if you turn that on in your project’s settings, only for failed requests to your own site, with anything under a secret-looking name replaced in the browser. The widget never sends request or response headers, cookies or console.log output, and it sets no cookies. It keeps an unsent report in the visitor’s own browser so it is not lost, and a sign-in token for your team members. On the free plan, the report form shows a small link to brokenhere.com.

Broken Here’s terms of service: https://brokenhere.com/terms
Broken Here’s privacy policy: https://brokenhere.com/privacy
sections.installation:
1. In your WordPress admin, go to Plugins › Add New Plugin, search for Broken Here, then install and activate it.
  2. Create a free account at brokenhere.com and add your site. Your project’s Setup shows its key, which starts with wq_.
  3. Go to Settings › Broken Here and paste the key. Pasting the whole script tag from Setup works too.
  4. Open your site. The Report issue button is in the bottom right corner, and your project’s Setup says Live.

If a caching plugin is active, clear its cache after saving, so visitors get pages with the button.
sections.faq:
Do the people reporting need an account?

No. They write a sentence and press Send. Adding their name or email is up to them.

Where do I find my project key?

On brokenhere.com, open your project, then Settings › Setup. The key starts with wq_.

Can I show the button only to my client?

Yes. Under Settings › Broken Here, choose Only people logged in to this site. Give your client a login to the site, and visitors see nothing.

Can I use my own link instead of the floating button?

Yes. Any link to #report-a-bug opens the report form: add a menu item, a button or a link with that address. To hide the floating button, set Button to No floating button, only my own links.

Can I move the button or change its colour?

Choose a corner under Settings › Broken Here. For the colours, add this to Appearance › Customize › Additional CSS (or Styles › Additional CSS in the site editor) with your own colour:

[data-wq-root] { --wq-accent: #2f6b4f; }

The customising guide lists every colour and font you can set.

Does it slow my site down?

No. The button loads asynchronously after your page. A small script in the page’s head keeps any error thrown while the page loads until the button arrives; it only listens.

Does it work with caching and optimization plugins?

Yes. Clear the cache after changing the settings. If your optimization plugin delays JavaScript until the visitor scrolls or taps, the button appears then. The small script that keeps errors from the start of the page load is marked so that WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, Jetpack Boost and Cloudflare’s Rocket Loader run it straight away; with another plugin that delays it, add broken-here-early to that plugin’s list of scripts not to delay.

Is it GDPR-friendly? Does it set cookies?

The button sets no cookies. Password fields are blurred in the visitor’s browser before the screenshot is taken, and addresses lose anything that looks like a secret before they are sent. Headers, cookies and console.log output are never collected. The details are under External services, below, and in what gets captured.

Does it work with WooCommerce and page builders?

Yes. The button is added to every page your theme prints, whatever built it.

What about multisite?

Each site in a network is a site in Broken Here, with its own key under its own Settings › Broken Here.

What happens to my reports if I delete the plugin?

They stay in Broken Here. Deleting the plugin removes its settings from WordPress and nothing else.
